name: Printing Consecutive Numbers Within a Specified Range (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that prints a sequence of numbers from 1 (inclusive) to 9 (inclusive).
code:
#Step 1: Iterate through the numbers in the sequence
for num in range(1, 10): 
    #Step 1.1: Print each number in the sequence
    print(num)

commentList: This line starts a loop that runs the indented block once for each number from 1 up to 9, so it provides the main control that produces the sequence you will print.

Breakdown: 'for' begins the loop; 'num' is the loop variable that takes each value; 'in' indicates iteration over a sequence; 'range(1, 10)' generates numbers starting at 1 and stopping before 10; the ':' marks the start of the indented loop body.
Common mistakes: you might expect range(1, 10) to include 10 — remember the stop is exclusive, so the last value is 9; also a missing ':' or incorrect indentation will cause a syntax error.
Other pitfalls: if you reuse the variable name 'num' later, you can accidentally overwrite it — in Python the loop variable keeps its last value after the loop (9), so avoid unexpected reuse.

Best practices: use a clear variable name, keep the ':' and indentation consistent, and only convert range to a list when you need indexing or multiple passes; if you want an inclusive upper bound, set the stop to upper+1.

commentList: You use print(num) to display the current loop value to the console; this is what produces the visible sequence 1 through 9, one number per line because print adds a newline by default.

You are calling Python's print function with num as the argument: num is evaluated to its integer value, converted to text, and written to standard output. In Python 3 you must use parentheses around the call; print itself returns None and does not modify num.

Watch out for common errors: writing print num (without parentheses) causes a SyntaxError in Python 3, using the wrong variable name (for example print(n)) raises a NameError, and wrong indentation can place this line outside the loop so you print only once instead of for every number.

As a best practice, keep print simple for learning and small scripts; if you want numbers on the same line use print(num, end=' ') or create a single string with ' '.join(...) for better performance when printing many items. For production code consider using logging instead of print.

distractors.description: You might pick this because it looks like you're starting at 1 and stopping at 9 — it feels natural to put 9 as the end. The misconception is that the end argument to range() is included in the sequence; in many students' first encounters they treat it as the last printed number. If you use this line, your program will print numbers 1 through 8 and omit the 9, so the output will be too short. Compared with the intended loop header, this distractor fails to include the final number you need; it uses an end value that causes the sequence to stop one step early, which is why it is incorrect despite seeming very similar.

You might choose this because it's shorter and you may think '10' will produce ten numbers from 1 to 10. The common error is assuming that range(n) begins at 1 instead of 0. If you run this line, the loop will start at 0 and print 0 through 9, so you'll get an extra 0 at the start and include 10 numbers instead of the intended sequence. Compared to the correct loop header, this distractor both starts at the wrong place and produces the wrong set of numbers, so the output will not match the desired 1-to-9 sequence.

You might pick this because you think adding a larger end value ensures the last desired number is included — a 'safer' upper bound. The mistake here is misunderstanding how the end argument controls inclusion; using 11 produces one extra number past what you need. With this line, the program will print 1 through 10, so it will include an unwanted 10 at the end and produce too many numbers. Compared to the intended loop header, this distractor goes beyond the intended final value, resulting in an extra printed number and an incorrect output range.
